easy.heading: A Breezy Morning Start
easy.body:
I started today's session with a nice cup of coffee and the easy puzzle, which was a lovely way to wake up the brain. The first thing that caught my eye was the small sum target of 1 at cell (3,1). In a game like Pips, a sum of 1 is a huge gift because it really limits what can go there. I quickly looked at my dominoes and saw the [4,1] which seemed like a great fit for the area near (3,1) and (3,2). 

Another helpful spot was the sum of 6 at (0,2) and (1,2). I had the [2,4] domino in my tray, and since 2 plus 4 equals 6, it was a perfect match. I also had to keep an eye on those empty spots at (0,3) and (2,3). They act like little roadblocks that help you figure out where the dominoes cannot be fully placed. By the time I placed the [3,5] domino across the bottom right, the whole grid just clicked together beautifully. It is all about finding those small sum anchors first!

medium.heading: Finding a Good Rhythm
medium.body:
The medium puzzle felt a bit more like a dance. The biggest challenge was definitely the sum of 10 at (3,2) and (3,3). Since we are working with pips, you know you need some of the highest values available. Looking at the domino list, the [4,6] was the obvious choice to hit that target. Once I got that big guy in place, I turned my attention to the equals region spanning (3,0), (3,1), and (4,1). 

Having three cells that all must share the same value is a big constraint. It forces you to look at how your dominoes are oriented. I found that using the [3,2] and [3,4] dominoes around that area helped satisfy the equals constraint while keeping the sums in check. The most satisfying part was finally fitting the [0,4] domino into (0,1) and (0,2). It felt like the last piece of a jigsaw puzzle. If you get stuck on this one, I recommend focusing on the longest equals chains first, as they dictate so much of the board's layout.

hard.heading: The Ultimate Logic Test
hard.body:
If you are looking for a challenge, the hard puzzle today definitely delivers. The grid was covered in these long equals regions that felt a bit intimidating at first. Specifically, that five-cell chain running from (2,4) all the way down to (6,4) was the puzzle's backbone. When you have five cells that all need to be the same number, you have to be very careful about which dominoes you use so you do not run out of matching values. 

I found my breakthrough near the bottom with the sum of 8 at (5,0) and (6,0). I tried a few combinations but the [3,5] domino ended up being the key. From there, I could trace the logic up through the other equals regions. There were a few moments where I thought I had hit a dead end, especially with the [5,6] and [4,6] dominoes, but shifting them slightly to satisfy the sum of 5 at (7,3) and (7,4) fixed everything. It is a bit like a row of dominoes falling in real life—once you get that first big chain right, the rest of the board follows suit. Take your time with this one and do not be afraid to backtrack if the numbers stop matching up!

easy.tips: Try to look for the smallest or largest sum targets first because they have the fewest possible combinations. Also, pay close attention to the equals regions that involve three or more cells, as these will usually tell you exactly which numbers you need to save for those spots.
easy.learned: Today I learned just how much the empty cells can help narrow down your choices. They might seem like they are just in the way, but they actually act as vital clues for where a domino must end. I also realized that long equals chains are actually your best friend because they limit the pool of usable dominoes very quickly.

faqs.question: How do you solve the sum regions in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: You solve them by placing domino ends into the highlighted cells so that the total number of dots equals the target number shown in that region.

faqs.question: What does an empty target cell mean in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: An empty target means that the cell is part of a region that does not have a specific sum or equality rule, often serving as a space that must be filled by a domino end without affecting a total.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for Equals constraints in Pips?
faqs.answer: The best strategy is to look at your available dominoes for pairs or doubles. Since every cell in an equals region must have the same number of dots, you need dominoes that can provide those matching values in a row.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes can only be placed horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent cells in the grid.

faqs.question: What should I do if I run out of dominoes before the grid is full?
faqs.answer: If you run out of dominoes or cannot fit the remaining ones, it usually means one of your earlier placements is incorrect. Try clearing the most recent dominoes and looking for a different way to satisfy the sum or equals constraints in that area.
